references.text: The parallel account in Matthew of the feeding of the five thousand, where Jesus tells the disciples "You give them something to eat!" and they reply that they have only five loaves and two fish.

The parallel account in Mark, where Jesus commands the disciples to give the crowd something to eat, and they ask if they should go and buy bread for two hundred denarii. They then find five loaves and two fish.
The parallel account in John, where Philip points out that two hundred denarii are not enough for bread for everyone, and Andrew mentions the boy with five barley loaves and two fish.

Elisha's feeding miracle where twenty barley loaves were given to a hundred men. The servant reacted with doubt, but the Lord said they would eat and have leftovers—a foreshadowing of Jesus' feeding miracles.

Moses asks the Lord how he can provide meat for six hundred thousand foot soldiers, doubting whether there are enough fish or small livestock—a similar situation where human inadequacy is set against God's provision.

At the feeding of the four thousand, the disciples again ask where they can get enough bread in the wilderness, and Jesus asks how many loaves they have—the same pattern of human limitation and divine provision.
At the feeding of the four thousand in Mark, the disciples ask how anyone can feed these people with bread here in the wilderness, and Jesus asks how many loaves they have.
